options.A: Flail leaflet from chordal rupture, shown by a tip pointing into the right atrium in systole.
options.B: Ebstein anomaly, shown by apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet relative to the mitral annulus.
options.C: Functional regurgitation from annular dilation, shown by normally inserted septal leaflets that fail to coapt centrally

explanation: The correct answer is B (Ebstein anomaly, shown by apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet relative to the mitral annulus.): Apical displacement of the septal leaflet by 8 mm/m2 or more, with an atrialized portion of the right ventricle, defines Ebstein anomaly. A flail leaflet shows loss of coaptation without displaced insertion. Functional disease has normally inserted leaflets that fail to coapt because of annular enlargement.

question: A 77-year-old man with serum potassium 3.4 mEq/L and magnesium 1.6 mg/dL is scheduled for TEVAR of a descending aneurysm. The team plans rapid ventricular pacing at 180 beats/min during deployment. Which approach is most appropriate to limit ventricular arrhythmia risk?

options.A: Proceed with pacing now, since brief pacing carries little arrhythmia risk with mild hypokalemia
options.B: Replete potassium and magnesium, pace through a temporary transvenous wire, and keep defibrillator pads applied
options.C: Use transcutaneous pacing at 180 beats/min, which avoids wire perforation and ventricular arrhythmia risk during deployment

explanation: The correct answer is B (Replete potassium and magnesium, pace through a temporary transvenous wire, and keep defibrillator pads applied): Rapid pacing can induce ventricular fibrillation, and low potassium and magnesium lower the threshold. Correcting electrolytes, using a secure transvenous wire or the stiff left ventricular guidewire, and having pads on are standard precautions. Transcutaneous capture at that rate is painful and unreliable.

question: A 71-year-old man separates from bypass after mitral valve repair with a ventricular rate of 130 beats/min in the rhythm shown on the tracing. Mean arterial pressure is 52 mmHg despite phenylephrine, and the heart is poorly filled. Which strategy best resolves the trade-off?

options.A: Synchronized cardioversion with internal paddles at 10 to 20 joules, since the rhythm is compromising hemodynamics
options.B: Amiodarone 300 mg bolus alone, since chemical conversion is quicker than cardioversion
options.C: Esmolol 500 mcg/kg bolus for rate control, accepting its negative inotropic effect on the recovering myocardium

image_params.caption: Lead II rhythm strip, 25 mm/sec, ventricular rate about 130 beats/min

explanation: The correct answer is A (Synchronized cardioversion with internal paddles at 10 to 20 joules, since the rhythm is compromising hemodynamics): Atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate and hypotension in a poorly filled ventricle means the atrial contribution is lost, and hemodynamic compromise calls for prompt cardioversion. Internal paddles use 10 to 20 joules. Esmolol would depress contractility when pressure is already low. Amiodarone takes time to act and can cause further hypotension, so it is an adjunct after conversion.

question: A 55-year-old man after aortic valve surgery has a radial arterial line reading systolic pressures 22 mmHg above simultaneous cuff values, with sharp spikes. Diastolic readings match the cuff. A fast flush test of the system is plotted in the chart. Which action best corrects the problem?

options.A: Re-zero the transducer at the phlebostatic axis, since the overshoot reflects a leveling error
options.B: Add a damping device to the tubing to reduce overshoot and ringing
options.C: Raise the pressure bag from 300 to 400 mmHg to speed continuous flush and flatten overshoot

explanation: The correct answer is B (Add a damping device to the tubing to reduce overshoot and ringing): The tracing oscillates repeatedly around the baseline before settling, which is typical of an underdamped system that exaggerates systolic pressure. Adding a damping device increases the damping coefficient into the optimal range. Raising bag pressure changes flush rate but not damping, and leveling errors shift the whole waveform without causing ringing.

question: A 55-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis, valve area 1.0 cm2, develops atrial fibrillation at 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg, and pulmonary edema while awaiting surgery. Urgent cardioversion is planned in the procedure room. Which anesthetic priority is most appropriate?

options.A: A large crystalloid bolus and esmolol infusion, converting later once pulmonary edema clears
options.B: Deep propofol sedation with phenylephrine infusion before cardioversion, since vasodilation is negligible in fixed mechanical obstruction
options.C: Prompt synchronized cardioversion with a reduced dose of a neutral sedative, since tachycardia shortens diastolic filling

explanation: The correct answer is C (Prompt synchronized cardioversion with a reduced dose of a neutral sedative, since tachycardia shortens diastolic filling): In mitral stenosis, rapid rates shorten diastole and raise left atrial pressure, so unstable fibrillation needs immediate restoration of rhythm. Sedation should avoid vasodilation and myocardial depression, which a large propofol dose would cause. Fluid loading worsens pulmonary edema, and slowing the rate with a negative inotrope before cardioversion delays definitive treatment.

question: A 62-year-old man on hemodialysis for six years needs aortic valve replacement. His life expectancy is estimated at about five years, and he has recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding from arteriovenous malformations. Which valve choice is most defensible in this particular situation?

options.A: A bioprosthetic valve, since uremia and hyperphosphatemia leave durability matching that of the general population
options.B: A mechanical valve, because bioprostheses calcify within a year in dialysis and warfarin bleeding is acceptable
options.C: A bioprosthetic valve, accepting faster deterioration, since limited life expectancy and warfarin bleeding risk outweigh durability

explanation: The correct answer is C (A bioprosthetic valve, accepting faster deterioration, since limited life expectancy and warfarin bleeding risk outweigh durability): Dialysis accelerates calcific degeneration of bioprostheses, but the patient's short expected survival and bleeding tendency make lifelong warfarin hazardous. Guidelines allow either valve in advanced kidney disease, and the individual circumstances here favor tissue. Deterioration within a year is an overstatement.

question: Three hours after aortic valve replacement for endocarditis with a root abscess, a patient has a new harsh holosystolic murmur, pulse-contour cardiac index 1.7 L/min/m2, mixed venous saturation 87 percent, rising lactate, and arterial saturation 97 percent. Which cause is most likely?

options.A: Impaired oxygen extraction from sepsis, since lactate is rising and the murmur reflects turbulent flow
options.B: A new ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunting, producing a right-sided saturation step-up
options.C: An overwedged catheter sampling pulmonary capillary blood, which would also produce a falsely low thermodilution output

explanation: The correct answer is B (A new ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunting, producing a right-sided saturation step-up): Left-to-right shunting through a postoperative VSD from the destroyed septum raises right-sided saturation while systemic output falls, and a new holosystolic murmur supports it. Sepsis can raise mixed venous saturation but does not explain the murmur. An overwedged catheter yields an invalid sample but not a new murmur.

question: A 62-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy, LVEF 25 percent, takes amiodarone 200 mg daily. During induction with etomidate, fentanyl and rocuronium for left ventricular assist device implantation, heart rate falls to 38 beats per minute and mean arterial pressure to 52 mmHg, with minimal response to glycopyrrolate. What is the best next step?

options.A: Start an epinephrine infusion and prepare pacing, because amiodarone blunts the response to anticholinergic drugs
options.B: Give a phenylephrine bolus and observe, since vasodilation from induction agents explains the slow heart rate
options.C: Repeat glycopyrrolate in higher doses until heart rate exceeds 60, since vagal tone dominates this bradycardia

explanation: The correct answer is A (Start an epinephrine infusion and prepare pacing, because amiodarone blunts the response to anticholinergic drugs): Amiodarone has sympatholytic and sinus nodal effects, so bradycardia during opioid-based induction may resist atropine and glycopyrrolate. A beta-agonist infusion such as epinephrine supports heart rate and contractility in a failing ventricle, with pacing available if that is inadequate. Repeating anticholinergic doses adds tachyarrhythmia risk without a dependable benefit. Phenylephrine raises afterload and can lower cardiac output further in a ventricle that depends on rate.

question: A 55-year-old man cannot be weaned two hours after orthotopic heart transplantation. Preoperative pulmonary vascular resistance was 5.2 Wood units. TEE shows a dilated hypokinetic right ventricle and underfilled left ventricle with no pericardial collection, and PA pressure is 62/30 mmHg with CVP 20 mmHg. What is the mechanism?

options.A: An unprepared donor right ventricle failing against elevated recipient pulmonary vascular resistance
options.B: Hyperacute antibody mediated rejection of the donor heart causing secondary pulmonary hypertension and right heart dilation
options.C: Cardiac tamponade from mediastinal bleeding compressing the right heart chambers

explanation: The correct answer is A (An unprepared donor right ventricle failing against elevated recipient pulmonary vascular resistance): A donor right ventricle has not adapted to chronically raised pulmonary resistance, and after ischemia and reperfusion it fails when faced with PA pressures of 62/30 mmHg. The dilated right ventricle with an underfilled left ventricle follows from this pressure overload. Hyperacute rejection does not originate in the pulmonary circuit. Tamponade is excluded by the absence of a pericardial collection on TEE.

question: A 60-year-old woman has microvascular bleeding after protamine following a long aortic root operation, with a mean pressure of 68 mmHg and temperature of 36.4 C. The exhibit shows a heparinase-neutralized thromboelastography and chemistry. Which product choice is most appropriate for this bleeding?

options.A: Cryoprecipitate 10 units alone, since low amplitude depends mainly on fibrinogen concentration
options.B: Plasma alone, since a prolonged R time explains the low amplitude
options.C: Plasma for the prolonged R time and platelets for the low amplitude

explanation: The correct answer is C (Plasma for the prolonged R time and platelets for the low amplitude): On a heparinase cup, a prolonged R time of 14 minutes indicates clotting factor deficiency, which plasma corrects. A low maximum amplitude of 42 mm with a normal fibrinogen of 380 mg/dL and a platelet count of 58 points to platelet deficiency, which needs platelets. Cryoprecipitate would add fibrinogen that is not lacking. Plasma alone leaves the platelet defect untreated.

question: A 60-year-old man is admitted with non-ST elevation myocardial infarction and critical left main stenosis. Abciximab was started with a bolus and infusion six hours ago. He is now pain free and hemodynamically stable, and the surgeon requests coronary bypass grafting. What is the most appropriate step regarding timing?

options.A: Stop the infusion and delay surgery about twelve hours while stable, because platelet function recovers slowly
options.B: Proceed immediately and transfuse platelets before incision to replace the inhibited platelets
options.C: Delay surgery for seven days, since receptor binding persists for the life of the platelet

explanation: The correct answer is A (Stop the infusion and delay surgery about twelve hours while stable, because platelet function recovers slowly): Abciximab binds the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor with a long dissociation time, and platelet function recovers over roughly 12 to 24 hours after stopping. In a stable patient, waiting allows recovery and reduces bleeding. Platelet transfusion gives limited benefit while free drug remains in plasma, and a seven day delay applies to irreversible P2Y12 inhibitors rather than abciximab.

question: A 58-year-old woman with a BMI of 42 has exertional dyspnea, preserved ejection fraction, and an average E/e' ratio of 17 on echocardiography. Her BNP is 95 pg/mL. A colleague says heart failure is excluded. How should this value be interpreted?

options.A: Obesity raises BNP through adipose secretion, so 95 pg/mL implies a higher true level confirming HFpEF
options.B: Obesity lowers natriuretic peptide levels, so this BNP does not exclude HFpEF and filling pressures matter
options.C: BNP below 100 pg/mL excludes heart failure in every body habitus, so investigate noncardiac pulmonary causes

explanation: The correct answer is B (Obesity lowers natriuretic peptide levels, so this BNP does not exclude HFpEF and filling pressures matter): Adipose tissue clears natriuretic peptides and obese patients have lower values for any given filling pressure, so thresholds underestimate disease. An E/e' above 14 supports elevated left ventricular filling pressure. The negative predictive value of BNP is reduced in obesity. Adipose tissue does not increase circulating BNP.

question: A 65-year-old man is on bypass for valve surgery with the laboratory values in the table. The cross-clamp is about to be released. He has a normal ejection fraction and received 3 L of cardioplegia. Which action should be avoided at this point?

options.A: Giving calcium once the heart is ejecting, guided by the ionized calcium measurement
options.B: Giving a calcium chloride bolus at clamp release, when calcium overload threatens the myocardium
options.C: Replacing magnesium, since low ionized magnesium predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias

explanation: The correct answer is B (Giving a calcium chloride bolus at clamp release, when calcium overload threatens the myocardium): Hemodilution and citrate lower ionized calcium and magnesium on bypass, and both can be replaced. Calcium bolus during the first moments of reperfusion can worsen intracellular calcium overload and reperfusion injury, so it is deferred until the heart is ejecting. Replacing calcium later and replacing magnesium are accepted practice.

question: A 66-year-old woman is hypotensive after esophagectomy with a mean arterial pressure of 58 mmHg. Cardiac output is measured at 3.6 L/min with a continuous monitor. A passive leg raise from the semirecumbent position raises cardiac output to 4.3 L/min within 90 seconds. How should this result be interpreted?

options.A: She is fluid unresponsive, because a rise below 25 percent shows exhausted preload reserve.
options.B: The result is uninterpretable, since passive leg raise shifts unstressed volume and cannot predict response.
options.C: She is fluid responsive, since the 19 percent rise reflects recruited stressed volume.

explanation: The correct answer is C (She is fluid responsive, since the 19 percent rise reflects recruited stressed volume.): A passive leg raise shifts about 300 mL of blood from the legs and splanchnic bed, converting unstressed to stressed volume, and acts as a reversible fluid challenge. The rise from 3.6 to 4.3 L/min is 19 percent, above the usual 10 to 15 percent threshold for fluid responsiveness. A 25 percent threshold is not the accepted cutoff. The maneuver is validated in hypotensive and ventilated patients, particularly with a real time cardiac output measurement.

question: A 69-year-old man with HFrEF, LVEF 30 percent and NYHA class III symptoms is scheduled for CABG in six weeks and reports worsening exertional fatigue. The table shows his iron studies and blood counts from clinic. Which is the best preoperative treatment to improve his anemia and symptoms?

options.A: Oral ferrous sulfate daily, since oral iron restores iron stores in heart failure within six weeks
options.B: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose, since ferritin below 100 ng/mL defines iron deficiency in heart failure
options.C: An erythropoiesis-stimulating agent alone, since it corrects anemia in heart failure without iron supplementation

explanation: The correct answer is B (Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose, since ferritin below 100 ng/mL defines iron deficiency in heart failure): In heart failure, iron deficiency is defined by ferritin under 100 ng/mL or ferritin 100 to 299 with transferrin saturation under 20 percent. Intravenous iron improves function and avoids the poor absorption of oral iron in this setting. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents without iron are ineffective in iron deficiency and add thrombotic risk.

question: A 64 year old man with a known cold agglutinin titer of 1:512 and a thermal amplitude of 30 C is scheduled for coronary bypass with a left internal thoracic graft. The team is planning cardioplegia and systemic cooling strategy. Which strategy should be avoided?

options.A: Infusing cold crystalloid cardioplegia into the coronary circulation without first flushing blood and warming the solution
options.B: Warming the operating room and administering prewarmed intravenous fluids and blood products throughout extracorporeal circulation
options.C: Using warm blood cardioplegia with systemic temperature kept near 34 C throughout the cross clamp period

explanation: The correct answer is A (Infusing cold crystalloid cardioplegia into the coronary circulation without first flushing blood and warming the solution): Cold agglutinins bind red cells at temperatures below the thermal amplitude, here 30 C, and cold cardioplegia can cause intracoronary agglutination, hemolysis and poor myocardial protection. Warm blood cardioplegia, limited systemic cooling and warmed fluids all keep blood above the thermal amplitude. Cold crystalloid cardioplegia without an initial warm flush is the approach to avoid.

question: A 58-year-old man begins bypass for aortic valve replacement with the arterial pump flow held constant at 4.6 L/min. The exhibit shows pump line pressure and radial mean pressure after starting. The surgeon notices a bluish discoloration in the aortic wall. What is the next step?

options.A: Increase pump flow to overcome the high line pressure and restore radial pressure
options.B: Give phenylephrine to raise radial pressure and continue bypass at the current flow
options.C: Slow or stop arterial inflow, then assess the aorta by TEE and inspection

explanation: The correct answer is C (Slow or stop arterial inflow, then assess the aorta by TEE and inspection): A rising pump line pressure with falling systemic pressure at constant flow suggests the cannula is obstructed or in a false lumen, and the bluish aortic wall is consistent with dissection. Continuing flow forces blood into the dissection plane, so inflow should be reduced or stopped and the cause identified by TEE and direct inspection. Raising flow or giving a pressor would worsen propagation.

question: A 26-year-old woman with Eisenmenger syndrome presents at 10 weeks gestation and asks about her risk. She is cyanotic with resting saturation 83% and takes sildenafil. Her cardiologist asks the anesthesiologist to join the counseling visit. Which statement is most accurate regarding maternal outcomes and counseling?

options.A: Maternal mortality is about 5 percent with modern care, so continuing pregnancy is reasonable
options.B: Maternal mortality is about 30 to 50 percent, so early discussion of termination is advised
options.C: Maternal mortality is about 15 percent, mostly from postpartum hemorrhage, so pregnancy is allowed with anticoagulation

explanation: The correct answer is B (Maternal mortality is about 30 to 50 percent, so early discussion of termination is advised): Pregnancy in Eisenmenger syndrome carries maternal mortality of about 30 to 50 percent, with deaths from right heart failure, thromboembolism, and sudden collapse, mostly around delivery and the early postpartum period. Pregnancy is therefore classified as contraindicated, and counseling includes early discussion of termination and contraception. Lower mortality figures reflect other lesions and do not apply, and anticoagulation does not make this pregnancy safe.

question: A 59-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis had the measurements in the exhibit. Before incision her transmitral mean gradient has doubled without any procedure on the valve, and her valve area was not remeasured. Which explanation is most likely for the change in her gradient?

options.A: Pressure half-time has lengthened with greater preload, which proves that the valve area has fallen significantly.
options.B: Progression of leaflet fibrosis over a few hours has reduced the valve area below 1.0 cm2.
options.C: The faster rate shortens diastolic filling time, raising the gradient with no change in valve area.

sections.heading: Clinic
sections.text: Heart rate 58 per min, mean gradient 6 mmHg, MVA 1.3 cm2 by half-time

sections.heading: Operating room, before incision
sections.text: Heart rate 96 per min, mean gradient 12 mmHg

explanation: The correct answer is C (The faster rate shortens diastolic filling time, raising the gradient with no change in valve area.): The gradient across a stenotic mitral valve depends on flow and diastolic filling time, so a faster rate shortens diastole and raises the gradient for the same area. Valve area does not change within hours. Half-time can also vary with rate and loading conditions, so a changed gradient alone does not signal progression.

question: A 54-year-old man listed for heart transplantation has pulmonary vascular resistance of 4.2 Wood units and a transpulmonary gradient of 14 mmHg that falls with nitroprusside. A donor offer is being evaluated. Which planning step best addresses the risk of postoperative right ventricular failure?

options.A: Accept a donor with ischemic time near six hours, since a stiffer pulmonary bed tolerates delay
options.B: Accept a donor with substantially lower body weight to reduce the ischemic injury during implantation
options.C: Request a size-matched or modestly larger donor and prepare inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol with milrinone

explanation: The correct answer is C (Request a size-matched or modestly larger donor and prepare inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol with milrinone): A donor right ventricle faces a recipient pulmonary circulation with elevated resistance, so donor size and ischemic time matter. A size-matched or somewhat oversized donor provides more reserve, and short ischemic time protects the right ventricle. Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators and inodilators should be ready at separation from bypass.

question: After 90 minutes of bypass with hypothermic arrest for arch replacement, a 63-year-old man has diffuse microvascular bleeding after protamine reversal. ACT is 128 seconds, platelets 62,000/mm3, fibrinogen 120 mg/dL and INR 1.7. Which blood product plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate and platelets first, then plasma guided by viscoelastic testing
options.B: Give additional protamine 100 mg, since ACT of 128 seconds shows persistent residual heparin anticoagulant effect
options.C: Give high-dose recombinant factor VIIa before any component therapy to correct this combined coagulopathy

explanation: The correct answer is A (Give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate and platelets first, then plasma guided by viscoelastic testing): The ACT is near baseline, so heparin is reversed and more protamine would add an anticoagulant effect. The bleeding follows platelet loss, hypofibrinogenemia and factor dilution after prolonged bypass and cold, and these are replaced specifically. Factor VIIa without replacing fibrinogen and platelets is ineffective and risks thrombosis.

question: A 29-year-old woman with a prior transvenous lead infection and no pacing indication is evaluated for a subcutaneous ICD. Surface ECG screening is performed supine and upright using the manufacturer template over the proposed sensing vectors. What does a passing screen primarily establish about her tracing before implantation?

options.A: A QRS to T wave amplitude ratio that limits T wave oversensing in one vector
options.B: A PR interval short enough to confirm intact atrioventricular conduction for dual chamber sensing
options.C: A QRS duration below 120 ms so antitachycardia pacing can be delivered reliably

explanation: The correct answer is A (A QRS to T wave amplitude ratio that limits T wave oversensing in one vector): The S-ICD senses far field signals, so the screen checks that the R wave is large relative to the T wave in at least one vector to avoid T wave oversensing and inappropriate shocks. The device has no antitachycardia pacing capability, so QRS duration does not determine that function. It also provides no atrial sensing, so PR interval is not what the screen tests. Patients who fail screening in all vectors are poor candidates.

question: A cardiac surgery program is building a pathway at a high-volume center based on the Enhanced Recovery After Cardiac Surgery Society recommendations for elective bypass patients with preserved ejection fraction and no major comorbidity. Which pair of elements is consistent with those recommendations?

options.A: Routine benzodiazepine premedication with a long-acting opioid infusion to maintain deep overnight sedation and ventilation
options.B: Strict bed rest for 48 hours, with mobilization deferred until all chest tubes are removed
options.C: Multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with regional blocks and acetaminophen, plus extubation within six hours

explanation: The correct answer is C (Multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with regional blocks and acetaminophen, plus extubation within six hours): The recommendations favor multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia including regional techniques, acetaminophen, and early extubation targeted within six hours, along with early mobilization. Benzodiazepines and deep overnight sedation increase delirium and ventilation time. Prolonged bed rest is contrary to early mobilization, which reduces complications and length of stay.

question: A 48-year-old man with a saddle pulmonary embolus is hypotensive. TEE shows a dilated right ventricle with a D-shaped septum and severe tricuspid regurgitation whose peak velocity is 2.8 m/s. Which interpretation of the regurgitation best fits this finding in this setting of acute right heart strain?

options.A: Primary chordal rupture with a flail septal leaflet, where equalized pressures give a falsely low velocity.
options.B: Annular dilation from acute right ventricular overload, with low velocity from limited pressure generation.
options.C: Chronic pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular hypertrophy, which would produce a jet velocity above 4 m/s.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Annular dilation from acute right ventricular overload, with low velocity from limited pressure generation.): An acutely overloaded right ventricle dilates, distorts the annulus and loses coaptation, giving significant regurgitation. A normal right ventricle can rarely generate a pulmonary artery systolic pressure above about 50 to 60 mmHg, so the jet velocity stays near 2.5 to 3 m/s. Chronic disease would show hypertrophy and a faster jet.

question: A 68-year-old woman receives 12 units of red cells, 12 units of plasma and 2 platelet pools during a hemorrhage after aortic dissection repair. Her blood pressure is falling and the QT interval is prolonged. Which should be monitored most closely?

options.A: Bladder temperature alone, since hypothermia is the only major hazard to hemodynamics
options.B: Serum bicarbonate alone, since citrate toxicity appears only as metabolic acidosis
options.C: Ionized calcium, because citrate in stored blood chelates calcium and depresses contractility

explanation: The correct answer is C (Ionized calcium, because citrate in stored blood chelates calcium and depresses contractility): Citrate anticoagulant in blood products binds ionized calcium, and during massive transfusion the liver cannot metabolize it fast enough, producing hypocalcemia with hypotension, reduced contractility and QT prolongation. Ratio-based resuscitation of 1 to 1 to 1 magnifies the citrate load, so ionized calcium is measured frequently and replaced to keep it above 1.1 mmol/L. Temperature and bicarbonate matter but do not explain this picture.

question: A 45-year-old man with type A aortic dissection has acute severe aortic regurgitation on intraoperative TEE. Continuous wave Doppler of the regurgitant jet shows a pressure half-time of 140 milliseconds, shorter than expected with chronic regurgitation of similar severity. What explains the rapid decline of the aortic to ventricular gradient?

options.A: A dilated, compliant ventricle accommodates the regurgitant volume, so pressures equalize slowly over a long interval
options.B: A noncompliant left ventricle fills quickly, so its diastolic pressure rises and equalizes with aortic pressure
options.C: Aortic diastolic pressure falls quickly because compensatory systemic vasoconstriction has not yet had time to develop

explanation: The correct answer is B (A noncompliant left ventricle fills quickly, so its diastolic pressure rises and equalizes with aortic pressure): In acute severe regurgitation the unadapted left ventricle is normal in size and stiff, so the regurgitant volume rapidly raises its diastolic pressure toward aortic diastolic pressure. This steep fall in gradient shortens the pressure half-time, often below 200 milliseconds and frequently near 100 to 150. Chronic regurgitation allows dilation and compliance, which lengthens the half-time. Vasoconstriction timing is not the primary determinant.

question: A 68-year-old man with COPD and an FEV1 of 40 percent of predicted fails extubation twice after distal arch repair. Chest radiograph shows an elevated left hemidiaphragm, and fluoroscopy shows paradoxical movement. His voice is only mildly hoarse. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Unilateral left recurrent laryngeal injury, which alone causes marked loss of vital capacity
options.B: Left phrenic nerve injury with hemidiaphragm paralysis compounding limited pulmonary reserve from COPD
options.C: Cervical spinal cord ischemia producing bilateral diaphragm weakness with early hypercapnia on the first postoperative day

explanation: The correct answer is B (Left phrenic nerve injury with hemidiaphragm paralysis compounding limited pulmonary reserve from COPD): Cold injury or traction near the pericardium can injure the left phrenic nerve, causing hemidiaphragm paralysis that is poorly tolerated in severe COPD. Fluoroscopy showing paradoxical movement of one hemidiaphragm supports this. Recurrent laryngeal injury impairs airway protection and voice but does not meaningfully reduce vital capacity, and bilateral diaphragm weakness does not fit a unilateral elevation.

question: A 66 year old woman with cold agglutinin disease, titer 1:2,048 and thermal amplitude 30 C, requires coronary bypass with a left internal thoracic graft. The antibody screen is positive at room temperature and she is otherwise stable. Which strategy is best for the operation?

options.A: Maintain warm systemic temperature with warm blood cardioplegia after a warm flush of the coronary circulation
options.B: Cool to 28 C with cold crystalloid cardioplegia and perform plasmapheresis only after the operation
options.C: Cool to deep hypothermia with circulatory arrest to minimize demand, adding warmed cardioplegia afterward

explanation: The correct answer is A (Maintain warm systemic temperature with warm blood cardioplegia after a warm flush of the coronary circulation): A thermal amplitude of 30 C means agglutination can occur whenever blood falls below that temperature. The surgical plan therefore avoids cooling, uses warm cardioplegia and warmed fluids, and flushes cold blood from the coronary circulation first. Cooling to 28 C or lower risks hemolysis and microvascular occlusion.

question: A 58-year-old man had an anterior STEMI four days ago and has left main plus three-vessel disease with an ejection fraction of 35%. Despite heparin, nitroglycerin, and beta blockade, he has recurrent angina with new ST depression, and an intra-aortic balloon pump has been placed. What is the most appropriate timing for CABG?

options.A: Operate only off bypass, since cardioplegic arrest is contraindicated within the first week after an infarct
options.B: Proceed with urgent CABG now, since refractory ischemia outweighs the added risk of early surgery
options.C: Delay surgery two more weeks to let the infarct heal, continuing balloon pump support and heparin

explanation: The correct answer is B (Proceed with urgent CABG now, since refractory ischemia outweighs the added risk of early surgery): Waiting for infarct healing is reasonable only when the patient is stable. Refractory angina with ST changes and left main disease despite maximal therapy indicates ongoing myocardium at risk, which justifies urgent revascularization. Cardioplegic arrest and bypass are not contraindicated early after infarction, although meticulous myocardial protection matters. A two-week delay exposes the patient to reinfarction and death.

question: A 70 year old man on postoperative day 6 after bypass has platelets falling from 210,000 to 88,000/mcL with a 4Ts score of 5. PF4 ELISA optical density is 0.9, weakly positive. The serotonin release assay result will take two days. Which statement best guides the immediate decision?

options.A: ELISA is highly specific, so a weak positive confirms HIT and the functional assay is unnecessary
options.B: ELISA is sensitive but poorly specific at low density, so stop heparin pending the functional assay
options.C: The serotonin release assay is less specific than ELISA, so continue heparin until density exceeds 2.0

explanation: The correct answer is B (ELISA is sensitive but poorly specific at low density, so stop heparin pending the functional assay): The PF4 ELISA detects antibodies with high sensitivity but low specificity, particularly at optical densities below 1.0, so many positive results do not cause HIT. The serotonin release assay detects platelet activating antibodies and is more specific, but results are delayed. With an intermediate pretest probability, stopping heparin and giving a nonheparin anticoagulant protects the patient while awaiting confirmation.

question: A 66-year-old woman had tricuspid valve annuloplasty and is in the intensive care unit. The tracing shows regular P waves unrelated to a slow regular ventricular rhythm of 38 per minute, and her blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. Atrial and ventricular epicardial wires were placed. Why are the epicardial wires most important at this moment?

options.A: They allow immediate temporary ventricular or AV sequential pacing while injured conduction tissue recovers
options.B: They deliver defibrillation energy directly to the ventricle if the escape rhythm degenerates into fibrillation
options.C: They permit overdrive pacing to terminate the junctional tachycardia caused by the annuloplasty

explanation: The correct answer is A (They allow immediate temporary ventricular or AV sequential pacing while injured conduction tissue recovers): The tracing shows AV dissociation with a slow escape rhythm, complete heart block, a known complication near the septal leaflet and the AV node after tricuspid repair. Epicardial wires let the team pace at once, ideally AV sequentially to preserve atrial contribution, while edema resolves. The rhythm is not a tachycardia, so overdrive pacing does not apply. Pacing wires cannot deliver defibrillation energy.

question: During aortic valve surgery the venous reservoir empties and a large volume of air is pumped into the arterial line and aorta before the pump is stopped. The patient is on bypass at 34 C. Which maneuver best clears air from the cerebral arteries?

options.A: Rapid rewarming to 37 C with hyperoxic ventilation so that intravascular bubbles dissolve readily into blood
options.B: Resume antegrade flow at 3 L/min/m2 to wash bubbles through the cerebral circulation
options.C: Head-down position with cold retrograde cerebral perfusion through the superior vena cava at moderate flow

explanation: The correct answer is C (Head-down position with cold retrograde cerebral perfusion through the superior vena cava at moderate flow): Stopping the pump, placing the patient head-down and perfusing cold blood retrograde through the superior vena cava flushes bubbles backward out of cerebral arterioles, and cooling raises gas solubility and lowers metabolic demand. Hyperbaric oxygen can follow afterward. Warming reduces solubility and expands bubbles. Vigorous antegrade flow drives more air distally into the cerebral microcirculation.

question: A 66-year-old man at a core temperature of 32 C has diffuse oozing after full protamine reversal. The exhibit shows laboratory and viscoelastic results, with the thromboelastography cup warmed to 37 C. What should the team expect from this assay?

options.A: A prolonged R time and low amplitude proportional to patient temperature will appear
options.B: A shortened R time will appear because cold platelets are hyperactive, masking enzyme slowing
options.C: The assay at 37 C looks near normal, underestimating the impairment present in the cold patient

explanation: The correct answer is C (The assay at 37 C looks near normal, underestimating the impairment present in the cold patient): Hypothermia slows clotting enzymes and impairs platelet function, but standard viscoelastic tests are run at 37 C, so they cannot reproduce the cold patient's defect and appear normal. The oozing despite normal values is the clue. Treatment is active rewarming to above 36 C. Cooling does not make platelets hyperactive, and the cup temperature does not follow the patient.

question: A 47-year-old man has been on venoarterial ECMO for four days. The exhibit shows oxygenator pressures and post membrane gas results from days one and four at the same blood flow, sweep and FiO2. Fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is rising. What is the best next step?

options.A: Raise sweep gas flow to 10 L/min to improve oxygen transfer across the membrane
options.B: Plan elective oxygenator exchange, since rising pressure drop and falling postoxygenator PaO2 indicate failing membrane
options.C: Increase blood flow to 5.5 L/min to lower the transmembrane pressure drop and restore oxygenation

sections.heading: Day 1
sections.text: Pre 240, post 210 mmHg; post membrane PaO2 450 mmHg

sections.heading: Day 4
sections.text: Pre 300, post 150 mmHg; post membrane PaO2 190 mmHg

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text: Blood flow 4.0 L/min, sweep 4 L/min, FiO2 1.0 on both days

explanation: The correct answer is B (Plan elective oxygenator exchange, since rising pressure drop and falling postoxygenator PaO2 indicate failing membrane): The pressure drop across the membrane rose from 30 to 150 mmHg while post oxygenator PaO2 fell from 450 to 190 mmHg at unchanged settings, which indicates clot accumulation and failing gas exchange. The solution is planned exchange of the oxygenator before it fails abruptly. Sweep gas controls carbon dioxide clearance, not oxygen transfer. Raising blood flow increases the pressure drop across a clotted membrane.

question: A 49-year-old man listed for heart transplant takes carvedilol and presents with cardiogenic shock: blood pressure 94/60 mmHg, cardiac index 1.7 L/min/m2, wedge 28 mmHg, and PVR 2.0 Wood units. Creatinine is normal and lactate is 3.1 mmol/L. Which inotrope is the best choice?

options.A: Dobutamine, since its inotropy is unaffected by long-term carvedilol and it avoids systemic vasodilation or hypotension
options.B: Milrinone, since its effect bypasses beta receptors blocked by carvedilol and it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance
options.C: Dopamine at 3 mcg/kg/min, since renal-dose dopamine raises cardiac output and preserves kidney function

explanation: The correct answer is B (Milrinone, since its effect bypasses beta receptors blocked by carvedilol and it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance): Carvedilol occupies beta receptors, which blunts dobutamine and epinephrine, whereas milrinone inhibits phosphodiesterase III downstream of the receptor and also reduces pulmonary resistance before transplant. Blood pressure should be watched, and vasopressin can offset vasodilation. Low-dose dopamine has no proven renal or output benefit.

question: A 66-year-old man with stable angina has an angiogram showing isolated left main coronary stenosis, and the heart team is deciding on revascularization. Which angiographic diameter stenosis defines significant left main disease and supports revascularization, with surgery preferred in suitable patients?

options.A: A diameter stenosis of 70 percent or greater, matching the cutoff used for other epicardial vessels
options.B: A diameter stenosis of 90 percent or greater, requiring near-occlusion before surgery is recommended
options.C: A diameter stenosis of 50 percent or greater

explanation: The correct answer is C (A diameter stenosis of 50 percent or greater): Left main stenosis of 50 percent or more is considered significant because the vessel supplies most of the left ventricle, and bypass surgery improves survival in this group. The 70 percent cutoff applies to non-left-main vessels. A near-occlusion threshold would withhold treatment from patients at high risk.

question: A 64 year old man arrives in the ICU after aortic valve surgery and receives protamine. Two hours later he has chest tube output of 220 mL/hr. The table shows ACT and TEG findings. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Clotting factor deficiency, treated with four units of fresh frozen plasma
options.B: Platelet dysfunction, treated with one apheresis platelet unit and desmopressin
options.C: Heparin rebound, treated with a small additional protamine dose of 25 to 50 mg

explanation: The correct answer is C (Heparin rebound, treated with a small additional protamine dose of 25 to 50 mg): A prolonged kaolin R time that corrects on the heparinase tracing, with a prolonged ACT after protamine, indicates residual or rebounding heparin released from tissue stores. A small additional dose of protamine neutralizes it. Normal platelet count, fibrinogen and heparinase R rule out factor or platelet causes.

question: During percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion, a 74-year-old woman becomes hypotensive to 66/38 mmHg with a heart rate of 124 per minute. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a rapidly enlarging pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse, and her ACT is 310 seconds. Which is the first intervention in the laboratory?

options.A: Urgent percutaneous pericardiocentesis with drain placement and autotransfusion of the aspirated blood
options.B: Full dose protamine alone, observing hemodynamics for 15 minutes before any pericardial drainage is attempted
options.C: A large volume crystalloid bolus of 2 L while preparing for thoracotomy in the operating room

explanation: The correct answer is A (Urgent percutaneous pericardiocentesis with drain placement and autotransfusion of the aspirated blood): Tamponade with rapid hemodynamic collapse needs immediate drainage, usually pericardiocentesis in the laboratory, with return of the aspirated blood through a venous line. Protamine reverses heparin and is given in parallel but cannot relieve the existing tamponade. Large crystalloid volumes dilute hemoglobin and clotting factors and delay definitive treatment. Surgical backup is notified in case of persistent bleeding.

question: A 55-year-old man on femoral venoarterial ECMO at 4.2 L/min for anterior STEMI shock now has pulse pressure under 10 mmHg, a closed aortic valve on echo, a wedge pressure of 30 mmHg, and pulmonary edema. Which addition is best?

options.A: Increase ECMO flow to 5.5 L/min to decompress the right atrium and reduce pulmonary vascular congestion
options.B: Left ventricular unloading with a percutaneous microaxial pump while maintaining ECMO flow
options.C: Add inhaled nitric oxide to lower pulmonary pressures and relieve the pulmonary edema

explanation: The correct answer is B (Left ventricular unloading with a percutaneous microaxial pump while maintaining ECMO flow): Peripheral venoarterial flow raises aortic afterload, and with a severely depressed ventricle the valve stays closed, so the left ventricle distends and the lungs flood. Venting through a microaxial pump, balloon pump, or atrial septostomy relieves the distension. Raising flow worsens afterload. Nitric oxide acts on the pulmonary arterial bed and does not decompress the left atrium.

question: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing hypothyroidism is evaluated for a large pericardial effusion discovered on routine imaging, and the exhibit summarizes her findings. She reports mild fatigue and no dyspnea, orthopnea or chest discomfort, and she is hemodynamically stable at rest. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Thyroid hormone replacement with serial echocardiography, since slow effusions without tamponade rarely need drainage
options.B: Urgent pericardiocentesis, because an effusion above 2 cm requires drainage to prevent progression to tamponade
options.C: Pericardial window under general anesthesia, since chronic myxedematous effusions of this size recur despite levothyroxine therapy

sections.heading: Echocardiography
sections.text: Large circumferential effusion 2.4 cm, no RA or RV diastolic collapse

sections.heading: Hemodynamics
sections.text: HR 72, BP 118/74 mmHg, CVP 8 mmHg, no pulsus paradoxus

sections.heading: Laboratory
sections.text: TSH 38 mIU/L, free T4 low, creatinine normal

explanation: The correct answer is A (Thyroid hormone replacement with serial echocardiography, since slow effusions without tamponade rarely need drainage): The exhibit shows no chamber collapse, normal pressures and no pulsus paradoxus, so there is no tamponade. Myxedematous effusions accumulate slowly, are tolerated well and usually resolve with thyroid replacement. Drainage is reserved for hemodynamic compromise or diagnostic need.

question: A 74-year-old man with a failed 21 mm stented surgical bioprosthesis is being evaluated by CT for valve in valve transcatheter replacement. The team reviews the aortic root measurements together. Which CT finding most strongly increases the risk of coronary obstruction?

options.A: A short stent frame height, because the leaflet tissue then lies well below the coronary ostia.
options.B: Coronary height under 10 mm, narrow sinuses, and virtual valve to coronary distance under 4 mm.
options.C: Coronary heights above 14 mm with sinuses wider than 32 mm and internally mounted leaflets.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Coronary height under 10 mm, narrow sinuses, and virtual valve to coronary distance under 4 mm.): Low coronary height, shallow sinuses of Valsalva, and a short virtual valve to coronary distance mean the displaced surgical leaflets can be pushed over an ostium. The left main is most often affected, and protective measures include a guidewire in the coronary or chimney stenting. High ostia with wide sinuses and short stent frames reduce rather than raise risk.

question: A 75-year-old man with a DDD pacemaker, lower rate 60 and upper tracking rate 120 per minute, develops sinus tachycardia at 140 per minute in the recovery unit. The device strip recording shows progressive lengthening of the paced AV interval followed by a dropped ventricular beat. Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: Device upper rate Wenckebach, appropriate behavior when the atrial rate exceeds the programmed upper tracking limit
options.B: Failure to capture from lead dislodgement, requiring an urgent output increase and a chest radiograph
options.C: Pacemaker mediated tachycardia from retrograde atrial sensing, requiring magnet application to terminate the reentrant circuit

explanation: The correct answer is A (Device upper rate Wenckebach, appropriate behavior when the atrial rate exceeds the programmed upper tracking limit): When sinus rate exceeds the upper tracking limit, the device lengthens the AV delay progressively to hold the ventricular rate, then drops a beat, a pattern called pacemaker Wenckebach. It is intended behavior and treating the sinus tachycardia, such as pain or hypovolemia, resolves it. Pacemaker mediated tachycardia is a regular rhythm at the upper rate. Failure to capture shows spikes without QRS complexes, not progressive AV delay.

question: A 70-year-old woman on dofetilide 500 mcg twice daily for atrial fibrillation is admitted for urgent mitral valve surgery. Her QTc is 520 ms, potassium 3.4 mEq/L and magnesium 1.5 mg/dL. She has no symptoms and a stable blood pressure. What is the best next step?

options.A: Give the scheduled dofetilide dose and add intravenous ondansetron for nausea prophylaxis before induction
options.B: Hold dofetilide, replete potassium above 4.0 and magnesium above 2.0 mg/dL, and monitor the QTc
options.C: Continue dofetilide at half dose and correct potassium alone, leaving magnesium for after bypass

explanation: The correct answer is B (Hold dofetilide, replete potassium above 4.0 and magnesium above 2.0 mg/dL, and monitor the QTc): Dofetilide prolongs repolarization, and hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia further raise the risk of torsades de pointes. The drug is held and both electrolytes are corrected to potassium above 4.0 and magnesium above 2.0 while QTc is followed. Ondansetron adds QT prolongation. Partial dosing with magnesium left uncorrected retains the risk.

question: A 54-year-old man is in the intensive care unit on postoperative day one after HeartMate 3 implantation. Central venous pressure is 24 mmHg, pump flow is 3.0 L/min, creatinine has risen from 1.4 to 2.3 mg/dL, and he is on epinephrine, milrinone and inhaled nitric oxide. Echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle. What is the best decision?

options.A: Add vasopressin and continue current support for 24 hours before reassessing right ventricular function
options.B: Place a temporary right ventricular assist device because failure persists despite inotropes and vasodilator
options.C: Raise milrinone to 0.75 mcg/kg/min and give a crystalloid bolus to improve left ventricular filling

explanation: The correct answer is B (Place a temporary right ventricular assist device because failure persists despite inotropes and vasodilator): Persistent venous congestion, low pump flow and worsening renal function on maximal medical therapy show established right ventricular failure after LVAD, which warrants temporary RV support such as CentriMag or ProtekDuo. More inotrope or vasopressin may help marginal cases, but waiting another day risks end-organ injury. Giving volume to a dilated, failing right ventricle raises central pressure further.

question: A 60-year-old man with severe aortic regurgitation is on cardiopulmonary bypass. Before the aortic cross-clamp is applied the heart fibrillates, and TEE shows rapid left ventricular distension with falling arterial pulse pressure. What is the mechanism, and what is the best immediate action?

options.A: Pump flow leaks through the incompetent valve into the empty ventricle; place a pulmonary vein vent.
options.B: Coronary sinus obstruction by the retrograde cannula distends the ventricle; deflate the balloon, give antegrade cardioplegia.
options.C: Bronchial venous return alone fills the ventricle; raise the reservoir height to improve right atrial drainage.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Pump flow leaks through the incompetent valve into the empty ventricle; place a pulmonary vein vent.): With a fibrillating ventricle and an incompetent aortic valve, arterial pump flow leaks backward into the left ventricle faster than it can be removed. Distension raises wall stress and damages myocardium, so a vent is placed to keep the ventricle decompressed. Root cardioplegia would worsen distension, and bronchial return is a minor contributor.

question: An anesthesiologist is setting up a five-lead ECG for a 64-year-old man undergoing elective coronary bypass and wants the pair of displayed leads with the best sensitivity for detecting intraoperative ischemia and arrhythmia. The monitor can display two leads simultaneously. Which pair should be displayed?

options.A: Leads I and aVL, since these reveal the lateral wall changes that dominate intraoperative ischemic events
options.B: Leads aVR and V1, since these best reveal septal ischemia and atrial rhythm
options.C: Leads II and V5: V5 is the most sensitive lead and II adds inferior ischemia detection

explanation: The correct answer is C (Leads II and V5: V5 is the most sensitive lead and II adds inferior ischemia detection): With only one precordial lead available on a five-lead system, V5 detects about 75 percent of ischemic episodes and lead II adds inferior ischemia and P waves for rhythm analysis, giving about 80 percent combined. The limb leads I and aVL and the leads aVR and V1 are less sensitive for intraoperative ischemia.

question: After coronary bypass with a radial artery graft to the obtuse marginal, a patient has diffuse ST elevation, blood pressure 75/40 mmHg, and poor graft flow on separation from bypass. Vasospasm is suspected and protamine has not yet been given. Which treatment is most appropriate?

options.A: Esmolol bolus to slow heart rate and lengthen the diastolic time available for graft filling
options.B: Phenylephrine bolus to restore perfusion pressure, since graft flow depends on pressure and spasm resolves spontaneously
options.C: Intravenous nitroglycerin with a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem, minimizing alpha agonist exposure

explanation: The correct answer is C (Intravenous nitroglycerin with a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem, minimizing alpha agonist exposure): Radial grafts and native vessels are prone to spasm, which is treated with vasodilators that act on arterial smooth muscle: nitrates and calcium channel blockers, with milrinone as an adjunct. Alpha agonists constrict arterial conduits and can worsen spasm. Beta blockade leaves alpha stimulation unopposed and gives no direct relief in a hypotensive patient.

question: A 24-year-old with hypertension and diminished femoral pulses undergoes echocardiography, and the suprasternal view shows turbulent flow in the descending thoracic aorta. The blood pressure is 165/90 mmHg in the right arm and the femoral pulses are delayed. Which Doppler finding indicates hemodynamically significant coarctation?

options.A: Retrograde diastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta, which indicates aortic regurgitation rather than coarctation
options.B: Continuous forward flow with a diastolic tail extending across the descending aorta, reflecting a persistent gradient
options.C: Peak velocity of 2.0 m/s with return to baseline in early diastole, indicating mild obstruction

explanation: The correct answer is B (Continuous forward flow with a diastolic tail extending across the descending aorta, reflecting a persistent gradient): In significant coarctation the pressure gradient persists through diastole, producing continuous forward flow with a diastolic tail on continuous-wave Doppler. A lower velocity with prompt return to baseline suggests mild or no obstruction. Diastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta is a sign of significant aortic regurgitation, not coarctation.

question: A transfusion committee is reviewing practice in a cardiac surgery unit where patients bleed after bypass. Anesthesiologists currently treat on the basis of PT, aPTT, platelet count and fibrinogen from the central laboratory, with turnaround of 45 minutes. Which statement best describes the tradeoff of a point-of-care viscoelastic algorithm?

options.A: Viscoelastic testing detects heparin effect and fibrinogen and has little value in platelet dysfunction
options.B: Results track laboratory PT and aPTT, so the algorithm shortens turnaround without changing product selection
options.C: Results arrive in minutes and reflect whole blood clotting, but assays are insensitive to P2Y12 inhibitors

explanation: The correct answer is C (Results arrive in minutes and reflect whole blood clotting, but assays are insensitive to P2Y12 inhibitors): Viscoelastic tests such as TEG and ROTEM assess the whole blood clot over time, including initiation, strength and lysis, and give actionable results within 10 to 15 minutes. Algorithms based on them reduce transfusion in bleeding cardiac patients compared with laboratory tests alone. Their limitation is poor sensitivity to P2Y12 inhibitor effect unless platelet mapping is used. They do reflect platelet contribution to clot strength and are not limited to heparin and fibrinogen.

question: A 52-year-old woman with NYHA class III symptoms has severe rheumatic mitral stenosis, area 0.8 cm2, heavily calcified leaflets with severe subvalvular fusion, moderate regurgitation, and a Wilkins score of 12. What is the best intervention to offer her at this point?

options.A: Surgical open commissurotomy, since leaflet calcification does not influence suitability for conservative valve repair.
options.B: Percutaneous balloon commissurotomy, since symptoms and area qualify and Wilkins scores up to 15 succeed.
options.C: Mitral valve replacement, because heavy calcification and subvalvular disease with regurgitation make valvotomy unlikely to succeed.

explanation: The correct answer is C (Mitral valve replacement, because heavy calcification and subvalvular disease with regurgitation make valvotomy unlikely to succeed.): Balloon valvotomy works best with pliable leaflets, low Wilkins scores around 8 or less, limited subvalvular disease, and no more than mild regurgitation. This patient has several unfavorable features, so replacement is the durable choice. Open commissurotomy also depends on pliable tissue.

question: A 75-year-old man with chronic hypertension is anesthetized for an aortic procedure. The arterial line reads 110/50 mmHg, intracranial pressure is 15 mmHg and central venous pressure is 12 mmHg. Using the standard definition of organ perfusion pressure, what is his cerebral perfusion pressure?

options.A: Cerebral perfusion pressure is 55 mmHg, calculated from mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
options.B: Cerebral perfusion pressure is 58 mmHg, calculated from mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure.
options.C: Cerebral perfusion pressure is 95 mmHg, calculated from systolic arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Cerebral perfusion pressure is 55 mmHg, calculated from mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.): Mean arterial pressure is the diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure, so 50 plus 20 equals 70 mmHg. Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus the higher of intracranial pressure and venous pressure, and here intracranial pressure of 15 mmHg exceeds central venous pressure, so 70 minus 15 equals 55 mmHg. Subtracting central venous pressure gives 58 mmHg, which uses the wrong back pressure. Using systolic pressure gives 95 mmHg, which is not a perfusion pressure.

question: A 71-year-old man weighing 80 kg with a serum creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL and an estimated GFR near 20 mL/min is scheduled for combined bypass grafting and aortic valve replacement. The team plans an antifibrinolytic. How should tranexamic acid dosing be approached in this patient?

options.A: Reduce the dose, since renal clearance predominates and accumulation raises the risk of seizures
options.B: Switch to aprotinin, since it carries no renal toxicity in patients with impaired function
options.C: Use the standard high-dose protocol, because hepatic metabolism clears most of the drug

explanation: The correct answer is A (Reduce the dose, since renal clearance predominates and accumulation raises the risk of seizures): Tranexamic acid is a lysine analog that blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin and is eliminated almost entirely by the kidney, so impaired GFR causes accumulation and a higher risk of postoperative seizures. Dose reduction is therefore needed. Hepatic metabolism is minimal, making the standard-dose rationale wrong. Aprotinin is associated with renal dysfunction, so it is a poor substitution here.

question: A 48-year-old man, an athlete with a normal heart, is anesthetized for a noncardiac procedure. The exhibit plots simultaneous radial and central aortic pressure tracings sampled across one beat. His radial systolic pressure reads 138 mmHg. Which interpretation of the exhibit is best?

options.A: Aortic systolic pressure exceeds radial systolic pressure because of distal arterial vasoconstriction and wave attenuation downstream.
options.B: Transducer resonance inflates the radial systolic value, so the aortic tracing should be discarded as erroneous.
options.C: Peripheral amplification makes radial systolic pressure higher than aortic, while mean and diastolic pressures stay similar.

explanation: The correct answer is C (Peripheral amplification makes radial systolic pressure higher than aortic, while mean and diastolic pressures stay similar.): As the pressure wave travels to the periphery, reflected waves and stiffer, narrower vessels raise systolic pressure and widen pulse pressure, so radial systolic pressure exceeds central aortic systolic pressure by 10 to 20 mmHg in young healthy adults. Mean and diastolic pressures change little. The exhibit shows two clean tracings with matching diastolic values, which argues against transducer artifact. Aortic systolic pressure is not higher than radial systolic pressure in this setting.

question: A 76-year-old man with exertional dyspnea has the transthoracic echocardiogram findings shown in the exhibit and is being considered for aortic valve replacement. His blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg. Which next step best distinguishes true severe aortic stenosis from pseudosevere stenosis?

options.A: Low dose dobutamine stress echocardiography to assess contractile reserve and recalculate valve area
options.B: Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in six months since a mean gradient below 40 mmHg excludes severe stenosis
options.C: Proceed to surgical valve replacement now, because a valve area below 1.0 cm2 confirms severe stenosis

sections.heading: Left ventricle
sections.text: LVEF 28 percent by biplane Simpson, end-diastolic diameter 62 mm

sections.heading: Aortic valve
sections.text: Heavily calcified, restricted leaflets. Peak velocity 3.5 m/s, mean gradient 28 mmHg

sections.heading: Derived values
sections.text: AVA 0.8 cm2, dimensionless index 0.20, stroke volume index 27 mL/m2

explanation: The correct answer is A (Low dose dobutamine stress echocardiography to assess contractile reserve and recalculate valve area): The exhibit shows a reduced ejection fraction with a low stroke volume index, so the low gradient may reflect low flow rather than mild disease. Dobutamine raises flow, and a true severe valve keeps a small area with a rising gradient, while pseudosevere stenosis shows an increasing area. Valve area alone cannot decide, and a low gradient does not exclude severe disease.

question: An adult with unexplained right heart enlargement undergoes an oximetry run, and the table lists the saturations. Mixed venous saturation is calculated as three parts SVC to one part IVC, the pulmonary vein sample is 98%, and the pulmonary artery sample is 85%. What is the approximate Qp:Qs and its meaning?

options.A: About 1.3, a small shunt that does not meet closure criteria
options.B: About 3.0, a large shunt that exceeds the pulmonary flow of a normal circulation
options.C: About 2.0, a significant left-to-right shunt at the atrial level

explanation: The correct answer is C (About 2.0, a significant left-to-right shunt at the atrial level): Mixed venous saturation is (3 x 70 + 76) / 4 = 71.5%. Qp:Qs equals (aortic 97 minus mixed venous 71.5) divided by (pulmonary vein 98 minus pulmonary artery 85), which is 25.5 divided by 13, or about 2.0. The step-up from SVC 70% to right atrium 84% localizes the shunt to the atrial level. A ratio of 1.3 or 3.0 does not follow from these values.

question: A 57-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has a peak transmitral velocity of 2.0 m/s, and the Doppler tracing shows a linear velocity decay. Using pressure half-time, read the time at which velocity reaches 1.41 m/s from the chart. What is the resulting valve area, and how is it classified?

options.A: About 2.3 cm2, calculated as 440 divided by the half-time, indicating only progressive stenosis.
options.B: About 0.7 cm2, calculated from the time at which velocity falls to half its peak.
options.C: About 1.2 cm2, which meets the 2020 criterion for severe stenosis of 1.5 cm2 or less.

explanation: The correct answer is C (About 1.2 cm2, which meets the 2020 criterion for severe stenosis of 1.5 cm2 or less.): The pressure half-time is the time for the gradient to fall to half, which corresponds to velocity falling to peak divided by 1.41, here 1.41 m/s at about 190 ms. The area is 220 divided by 190, or about 1.2 cm2, which is severe by the 2020 criteria of 1.5 cm2 or less. Using half of the velocity or a constant of 440 gives incorrect values.

question: A 64-year-old man is cooled to 32 C for coronary bypass and transesophageal imaging shows a severely calcified ascending aorta. Cerebral autoregulation is expected to be intact. He has no carotid disease. Which acid-base management strategy is best during cooling for this adult patient?

options.A: Alpha-stat management, preserving autoregulation and avoiding excess cerebral flow that delivers more emboli
options.B: pH-stat management with added carbon dioxide, to increase cerebral flow and cool the brain more uniformly
options.C: Permissive hypocapnia to a PaCO2 of 25 mmHg at 37 C, to limit embolic delivery

explanation: The correct answer is A (Alpha-stat management, preserving autoregulation and avoiding excess cerebral flow that delivers more emboli): Alpha-stat leaves cerebral autoregulation intact, so cerebral blood flow stays coupled to metabolism and embolic load delivered to the brain is lower than with pH-stat. With a calcified aorta and adult cerebral physiology, that is the better choice. pH-stat raises cerebral flow and abolishes autoregulation. Deliberate hypocapnia reduces flow below metabolic need and risks cerebral ischemia.

question: A 60-year-old man has asymptomatic chronic severe aortic regurgitation with a normal ejection fraction and blood pressure 170/60 mmHg despite diet changes. His physician asks which antihypertensive class is preferred in this valve lesion. Which choice is most appropriate for long term management?

options.A: High dose beta blocker, since a slower rate prolongs diastole and lowers regurgitant volume.
options.B: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or ACE inhibitor, to treat systolic hypertension and reduce regurgitant fraction.
options.C: Nitrate vasodilator to reduce preload, since decreased filling shrinks the ventricle and improves forward flow.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or ACE inhibitor, to treat systolic hypertension and reduce regurgitant fraction.): Lowering systemic resistance reduces the regurgitant fraction and the load on the left ventricle. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the recommended agents in hypertensive patients. Beta blockers prolong diastole and increase regurgitant volume, and nitrates mostly reduce preload without addressing afterload.

question: A 55-year-old man with exertional dyspnea and peripheral edema undergoes catheterization during cardiac transplant evaluation. Simultaneous ventricular tracings show a sharp early diastolic dip followed by a plateau, with left and right end-diastolic pressures within 3 mmHg of each other. Which process do these findings most strongly suggest?

options.A: Severe mitral stenosis, with a persistent diastolic gradient between the left atrium and left ventricle
options.B: Amyloid infiltration, with brisk early filling that ends abruptly in a stiff ventricle
options.C: Cardiac tamponade, with pulsus paradoxus and a blunted y descent in the right atrial tracing

explanation: The correct answer is B (Amyloid infiltration, with brisk early filling that ends abruptly in a stiff ventricle): A stiff, noncompliant ventricle fills rapidly in early diastole and then reaches its volume limit abruptly, producing the dip and plateau with equalized end-diastolic pressures. Tamponade also equalizes pressures but eliminates the y descent and lacks an early dip. Mitral stenosis produces a persistent gradient between left atrium and ventricle rather than equalization of ventricular pressures.

question: A 58-year-old man with unstable angina, a pending bypass operation, and 3+ aortic regurgitation on echocardiography is being considered for intra-aortic balloon pump support before surgery because of recurrent ischemia. Why is the balloon pump generally avoided in this setting?

options.A: Diastolic inflation raises aortic diastolic pressure and increases regurgitant volume, distending the left ventricle further
options.B: Systolic balloon deflation produces strong aortic suction that pulls blood backward across the valve
options.C: Balloon inflation obstructs the coronary ostia, shifting regurgitant flow toward the right ventricle

explanation: The correct answer is A (Diastolic inflation raises aortic diastolic pressure and increases regurgitant volume, distending the left ventricle further): The pump inflates during diastole to raise coronary perfusion pressure, but in aortic regurgitation that higher diastolic pressure drives more blood back into the ventricle. Left ventricular volume and wall stress rise, offsetting the intended benefit. Moderate or severe regurgitation is therefore a standard contraindication.

question: A 21-year-old presents for noncardiac surgery after staged palliation for hypoplastic left heart syndrome, including a Norwood operation, a bidirectional Glenn shunt, and a completed Fontan. The anesthesiologist reviews the surgical history to define the circulation. Which description best fits the anatomy and ventricle?

options.A: A single morphologic left ventricle supports the circulation through the native aorta, with Fontan drainage
options.B: Two ventricles share output in parallel, with an atrial switch and a conduit to the lungs
options.C: A single morphologic right ventricle supports the systemic circulation through a neoaorta, with Fontan venous drainage

explanation: The correct answer is C (A single morphologic right ventricle supports the systemic circulation through a neoaorta, with Fontan venous drainage): In hypoplastic left heart syndrome the left ventricle is too small, and the right ventricle becomes the single systemic ventricle after Norwood reconstruction, which builds a neoaorta from the pulmonary root and aortic arch. Subsequent Glenn and Fontan operations route systemic venous blood directly to the lungs. The left ventricle is not used as the systemic pump, and the circulation is not a biventricular arrangement.

question: A 55-year-old man develops ventricular fibrillation during a noncardiac procedure. Pads are placed and the team uses a biphasic defibrillator, but the manufacturer recommendation for initial energy is not known to the staff. What initial energy should be delivered for the first shock?

options.A: The maximum available energy of the biphasic device, typically 200 J
options.B: 50 J initial shock with escalation by 50 J increments after each failed attempt
options.C: 360 J, since biphasic devices require monophasic equivalent energy for initial defibrillation of ventricular fibrillation

explanation: The correct answer is A (The maximum available energy of the biphasic device, typically 200 J): The AHA advises using the manufacturer recommended biphasic energy, usually 120 to 200 J, and if that is unknown, using the maximum available dose, commonly 200 J. A low dose of 50 J has poor first shock success. Biphasic waveforms achieve defibrillation at lower energies than monophasic ones, so 360 J is not needed as a rule.

question: A 49-year-old man six weeks after HeartMate 3 implantation has flow fall from 4.8 to 2.4 L/min at constant speed while power falls from 4.7 to 3.1 W. Hemolysis labs are normal, CVP is 8 mmHg, and TEE shows a small left ventricle with the inflow cannula contacting trabeculae. What is the most likely complication?

options.A: Outflow graft kinking, which increases power with low flow and a dilated left ventricle
options.B: Pump thrombosis, since this pattern of low flow and low power reflects clot on the rotor
options.C: Inflow cannula obstruction, since low flow with falling power points to reduced blood entering the pump

explanation: The correct answer is C (Inflow cannula obstruction, since low flow with falling power points to reduced blood entering the pump): Low flow with falling power at fixed speed means less blood is reaching the rotor, as occurs when the inflow cannula is blocked by trabeculae, thrombus or malposition. TEE contact with trabeculae in a small ventricle supports this. Pump thrombosis typically shows rising power and hemolysis, and outflow graft obstruction shows a dilated ventricle with a changed power pattern. Both are excluded by the normal hemolysis labs and small cavity.

question: A 31-year-old man who injects drugs has Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia that persists after seven days of appropriate antibiotics. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 2.5 cm tricuspid vegetation and recurrent septic pulmonary emboli are evident on chest imaging. Which surgical management is preferred?

options.A: Continued antibiotics alone for six weeks, since right-sided vegetations rarely embolize or require operation
options.B: Mechanical tricuspid valve replacement with lifelong warfarin for durable infection control
options.C: Vegetectomy with tricuspid valve repair, preserving the native valve whenever the anatomy allows

explanation: The correct answer is C (Vegetectomy with tricuspid valve repair, preserving the native valve whenever the anatomy allows): Persistent bacteremia and recurrent septic emboli with a large vegetation are indications for surgery. In patients who inject drugs, repair or vegetectomy is preferred because it avoids placing a prosthesis in a setting of likely reinfection. Mechanical valves in the tricuspid position carry a high thrombosis risk, and continued medical therapy has already failed.

question: After mitral valve replacement in a 61-year-old man, transesophageal imaging shows a paravalvular jet with rocking of the prosthesis. The jet origin spans 25 percent of the sewing ring circumference, and he has a falling hematocrit with dark urine. How should this be interpreted?

options.A: Moderate leak, since extent under 30 percent grades moderate, observation with diuretics and surveillance echocardiography suffices
options.B: Severe leak by circumferential extent, with rocking suggesting dehiscence that needs surgical or percutaneous repair
options.C: Mild leak, since grading depends on vena contracta width alone and rocking is normal after replacement

explanation: The correct answer is B (Severe leak by circumferential extent, with rocking suggesting dehiscence that needs surgical or percutaneous repair): Paravalvular regurgitation is graded partly by the fraction of the sewing ring circumference involved, with more than 20 percent considered severe. Rocking of the prosthesis indicates a large dehiscence. Such leaks cause hemolysis and heart failure and usually need repair.

question: A patient had a HeartMate 3 implanted this morning and remains on epinephrine 0.05 mcg/kg/min. The exhibit shows hemodynamics and echocardiography at the end of the operation. Inhaled epoprostenol is started. Which change is expected over the next 20 minutes?

options.A: Pulmonary vascular resistance falls, right ventricular afterload decreases, and left ventricular filling and pump flow rise
options.B: Systemic vascular resistance falls substantially, lowering mean arterial pressure while pulmonary pressures remain unchanged
options.C: Pulmonary vascular resistance rises from ventilation-perfusion mismatch, so right ventricular afterload and pump flow both fall

sections.heading: Pressures
sections.text: PA 52/30 mmHg, mean 38; wedge 10 mmHg; CVP 20 mmHg

sections.heading: Pump
sections.text: HeartMate 3 at 5200 rpm, flow 3.1 L/min

sections.heading: Echo
sections.text: Dilated right ventricle, septum midline, small left ventricle

explanation: The correct answer is A (Pulmonary vascular resistance falls, right ventricular afterload decreases, and left ventricular filling and pump flow rise): The exhibit shows high pulmonary artery pressures and a central venous pressure of 20 mmHg with a dilated right ventricle and low LVAD flow, reflecting elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Inhaled epoprostenol selectively vasodilates ventilated lung units, so right ventricular afterload falls, more blood reaches the left heart, and pump flow increases. Inhaled agents have minimal systemic effect.

question: A 57-year-old woman with severe mitral regurgitation has an intraoperative TEE assessment of the mitral valve leaflets. The exhibit gives the TEE description of leaflet motion in systole and the direction of the regurgitant jet. Which Carpentier type best fits these findings?

options.A: Type II, excess leaflet motion with prolapse above the annular plane.
options.B: Type I, normal leaflet motion with annular dilation or leaflet perforation.
options.C: Type IIIb, restricted systolic leaflet motion from ventricular tethering.

sections.heading: Posterior leaflet
sections.text: P2 systolic tip position 6 mm cranial to the annular plane

sections.heading: Anterior leaflet
sections.text: Normal excursion, coaptation lost centrally

sections.heading: Jet and annulus
sections.text: Jet directed anteriorly, annulus 3.2 cm

explanation: The correct answer is A (Type II, excess leaflet motion with prolapse above the annular plane.): Carpentier type II describes excessive leaflet motion, where the leaflet edge rises above the annular plane, as with prolapse or flail. Type I involves normal motion, and type III involves restricted motion, either in diastole as in rheumatic disease or in systole from tethering. The jet points away from the prolapsing leaflet, here anteriorly.

question: A 48-year-old woman with a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve, atrial fibrillation and a prior embolic stroke takes warfarin and needs elective ascending aortic surgery in one week. Her INR is 3.1. Which anticoagulation plan best balances thrombotic and bleeding risk?

options.A: Stop warfarin and give no bridging, since bileaflet valves carry the same embolic risk as bioprostheses
